record.paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
record.context_brief: LoRa link-quality and coverage estimation models
record.original_question: How can LoRa networking obtain mathematical models and systems for estimating link quality and communication coverage across diverse deployment environments, including open-air locations, concrete- or steel-obstructed locations, homes, hospitals, schools, forests, line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight conditions, signal attenuation, propagation losses, fading, and anisotropic coverage caused by dynamic and static obstacles in different directions?

evidence.quote: LoRa networking will be deployed in many scenarios such as homes, hospitals, schools, forest, etc. end-devices will be placed in the locations open to air, closed by concrete or steel, etc. Aiming such diverse deployment conditions, signal attenuation, propagation losses and fading have to be countered to improve signal penetration thus improving the coverage of LoRa networks [35], [32].
Another important challenge is estimating the coverage of LoRa networks.

Demetri et al. [78] identiﬁed that LoRa’s signal coverage is anisotropic. This is because LoRa signals travel a longer distance and experience varying environments with dynamic and static obstacles in different directions. Mathematical models and systems for link quality estimation are still unexplored for LoRa.

It is also claimed that Bor’s model [21] need on-site measurements which is hard due to that most of the covered regions comprise of transitional links, which are deﬁned as links with dynamic temporal link qualities.

artifact.category_tag: Wireless channel modeling and coverage estimation
artifact.status_search_result: Several works have proposed partial solutions: remote-sensing-based automated link-quality estimation combining multispectral imagery with the Okumura-Hata model (Demetri et al., IPSN 2019); a First Fresnel Zone log-normal shadowing model classifying mediums along the path; FLog and related orchard-specific models; and SVM/kernel-based machine-learning estimators using RSSI, SNR, and PRR. These address aspects of anisotropy and heterogeneous environments, but a unified, rigorously validated mathematical framework with provable accuracy across all deployment scenarios (indoor, NLOS, forested, urban, transitional) remains an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Automated Estimation of Link Quality for LoRa: A Remote Sensing Approach
status_evidence.snippet: Combines multispectral remote-sensing imagery with the Okumura-Hata channel model to classify the environment traversed by each LoRa link and estimate link quality without on-site measurements.
status_evidence.claim: Provides a partial mathematical/data-driven model for LoRa link quality across heterogeneous environments.

status_evidence.title: Link Quality Modeling for LoRa Networks in Orchards
status_evidence.snippet: Uses a First Fresnel Zone log-normal shadowing model with per-medium path-loss exponents for vegetated environments.
status_evidence.claim: Addresses anisotropic, environment-specific link-quality modeling in a restricted setting.

status_evidence.title: FLog: Automated Modeling of Link Quality for LoRa Networks in Orchards
status_evidence.snippet: Automates LoRa link-quality modeling for orchards, extending Fresnel-zone-based shadowing models.
status_evidence.claim: A recent partial solution targeted at specific environments.

status_evidence.title: LoRa Link Quality Estimation Based on Support Vector Machine
status_evidence.snippet: Kernel SVM estimator using RSSI, SNR, and PRR features.
status_evidence.claim: Machine-learning approach to link quality, complementary to physical models.

status_evidence.title: A Study of LoRa Coverage: Range Evaluation and Channel Attenuation Model
status_evidence.snippet: Empirical channel attenuation model and range evaluation for LoRa.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical coverage modeling, partial progress on the coverage estimation problem.
